score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong Promise-Theory framing: a durable evidence index about who promised what, with later local observations, fits the scenario better than conformance-ledger language. It can support Bob making different adoption promises to Alice and Carol, but the current docs do not yet make relationship scope a first-class field, so scenario fit is good rather than complete.
strengths: Explicit promise/evidence/observation framing aligns well with Promise Theory.
Clear evidence-only boundary avoids central authority or certification semantics.
High auditability from exact evidence-object citation and later outcome recording.
Supports local trust judgments and preserves ambiguity/refusal as observable states.
weaknesses: Relationship-scoped adoption is not explicit in the simulation text.
Scenario coverage depends on implementers preserving counterparty/context in each entry.
Failure behavior for conflicting relationship-specific promises is not deeply specified.
risks: Relationship context may be implicit and later collapsed into peer-identity-only interpretations.
The index could drift back toward a quasi-certification ledger if implementations overstate what evidence entries mean.
Different peers may cite the same pCID with incompatible relationship-specific meanings unless scope encoding is explicit.
open_questions: Should each index entry carry an explicit relationship/counterparty scope so Bob->Alice and Bob->Carol adoption promises cannot be conflated?
Is relationship-scoped adoption represented inside the promised payload, in surrounding metadata, or in the local observation record?
What minimal durable fields are needed to preserve relationship context without turning the index into a larger profile or policy ledger?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: Entries describe what specific agents promised or observed; the index does not command peers or remove autonomy.

scoped_intent.note: pCID-scoped promise evidence fits scoped declarations of intent, though relationship scope for adoption should be made more explicit for this scenario.

no_promises_for_others.note: It records who made a promise and what evidence supports it, instead of letting one agent promise on behalf of another.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: The index is descriptive evidence only and can record keep, break, refusal, or ambiguity rather than guaranteeing results.

local_trust_assessment.note: The simulation explicitly leaves trust as a local judgment for Alice, Bob, or Carol.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: The design records promises and observations about use/adoption without converting receipt or use into obligation semantics.
